articleBody:
Im Rechtsstreit zwischen Finanzfluss und Meta hat das Landgericht Frankfurt geurteilt: Der Social-Media-Konzern steht in der Verantwortung für betrügerische Anzeigen. Im Interview erklärt Finanzfluss-Gründer Thomas Kehl, warum er geklagt hat und was das Urteil bedeutet.

Betrüger:innen schalteten auf den Social-Media-Plattformen Instagram und Facebook Scam-Werbung – Gemeinfrei-ähnlich freigegeben durch unsplash.com: dole777
Finanzfluss versteht sich als Bildungs- & Informationsplattform zum Thema Finanzen. Mit aktuell 1,65 Millionen Abonnent:innen zählt ihr YouTube-Kanal zu den größten dieser Art im deutschsprachigen Raum. Seit zehn Jahren ist Finanzfluss auf verschiedenen Social-Media-Plattformen aktiv und bietet neben Verbraucherratgebern, Testberichten und Einschätzungen auch verschiedene Werkzeuge wie etwa Zins- oder Vergleichsrechner an.

Ab 2024 tauchten auf Instagram und Facebook immer wieder Anzeigen auf, die Finanzfluss durch Name, Logo oder Bild imitierten. Mit Versprechen wie exklusiven Anlagetipps wurden Nutzer:innen in private Chatgruppen gelockt, wo vermeintliche Investments angeboten wurden. Finanzfluss meldete mehr als tausend Anzeigen von über 300 Accounts – es dauerte teils bis zu zwei Monate bis zur Löschung. Und sie sind nicht allein mit dem Problem: Interne Schätzungen von Meta gingen davon aus, dass 2024 rund zehn Prozent der Einnahmen aus betrügerischer Werbung stammten.

Ein außergerichtlicher Austausch von Finanzfluss und Meta blieb ergebnislos. Daraufhin reichten das hinter Finanzfluss stehende Unternehmen Finflow GmbH gemeinsam mit dem Geschäftsführer und Gründer Thomas Kehl im Sommer 2025 Klage ein. Das Landgericht Frankfurt hat dieser mit dem Urteil vom 16. September stattgegeben.

„Sie nutzen das Vertrauen, das die Leute in unsere Arbeit haben“

netzpolitik.org: Was war genau der Inhalt eurer Klage?

Thomas Kehl: Es ging um betrügerische Anzeigen. Wir haben Meta zur Unterlassung aufgefordert und wollten ein Auskunftsrecht geltend machen. So wollten wir erfahren, wie und in welchem Umfang diese Werbung verbreitet wurde und wie viel Geld Meta damit verdient hat. Auf der Grundlage fordern wir Schadensersatz.

netzpolitik.org: Was ist die Betrugsmasche?

Thomas Kehl: Die Betrügenden erstellen Scam-Anzeigen mit meinem Bild oder mit Bezug zu Finanzfluss. Sie verwenden etwa unsere YouTube-Thumbnails. Sie nutzen das Vertrauen, das die Leute in unsere Arbeit haben. Die Scammer bauen über Wochen sukzessive Accounts auf und fördern die Reichweite der Accounts durch große Werbebudgets. Dadurch gehen an einem einzigen Tag massenhaft Anzeigen live. Diese zielen auf unsere Finanzfluss-Community. Wer dahintersteckt, lässt sich von außen kaum nachvollziehen. Soweit wir es sehen können, handelt es sich oft um Briefkastenfirmen im asiatischen Raum.

netzpolitik.org: Wie habt ihr von dem Betrug erfahren?

Thomas Kehl: Internetaffine Mitglieder unserer Community haben es gemerkt und uns gemeldet. Wir haben auch mit zwei Betroffenen gesprochen, die tatsächlich Geld verloren haben. Beide sprechen Deutsch nicht als Muttersprache. Dadurch war die Betrugsmasche für sie noch schwerer zu durchschauen.

„Die Meldefunktion war gefühlt zwecklos“

netzpolitik.org: Wie seid ihr mit Meta umgegangen?

Thomas Kehl: Wir haben jede Anzeige über die Meldefunktion gemeldet. Das war gefühlt zwecklos. Meta hat uns ein sogenanntes Brand Protection Tool zur Verfügung gestellt, das überhaupt nicht protected. Manche Anzeigen wurden erst viele Tage nach der Meldung entfernt. In der Zwischenzeit fallen sehr viele Leute auf die Masche rein.

Teilweise wurden unsere Beschwerden auch abgelehnt und die Anzeigen verschwanden erst später.

–––

Gegen Ausweiskontrollen im Netz. 
Wir kämpfen für ein offenes Internet. Das geht nur mit deiner Unterstützung.

–––

netzpolitik.org: Wie war euer Umgang mit den Betroffenen?

Thomas Kehl: Wir haben jedem Betroffenen, der uns angeschrieben hat, empfohlen, Strafanzeige zu erstatten.

netzpolitik.org: Wie hoch sind die Schäden bei den Betroffe­nen?

Thomas Kehl: Wir haben mit einer Person gesprochen, die rund 50.000 Euro verloren hat. In der Summe lässt sich der Schaden nicht beziffern, die Dunkelziffer ist groß. Viele schämen sich, weil sie sich selbst für „so dumm“ halten, darauf hereingefallen zu sein. Ich würde das niemandem vorwerfen. Es ist nämlich nicht mehr diese plumpe Masche von früher. Heute wird das mit KI-generierten Videos und gefälschten Chats sehr professionell gemacht.

netzpolitik.org: Was war die Haltung der Geschädigten, als sie euch kontaktiert haben? Wie seid ihr damit umgegangen?

Thomas Kehl: Die Person, die 50.000 Euro verloren hat, hat mich auf LinkedIn angeschrieben, nachvollziehbarerweise ziemlich wütend. Sinngemäß: Wegen deiner Aktientipps bin ich ruiniert, wir müssen sprechen. Ich habe geantwortet: Das tut mir sehr leid, aber wir geben grundsätzlich keine Aktientipps. Danach schickte er mir Screenshots von WhatsApp-Chats mit „Thomas Kehl“. Da war schnell klar, dass Leute mich imitiert haben.

netzpolitik.org: Wie kann man wissen, wann es sich um Fake-Anzeigen oder ‑Profile handelt?

Thomas Kehl: Wir haben eine klare Regel für unsere Community: Wir schalten keine Werbung. Wenn irgendwo „Finanzfluss“-Werbung auftaucht, geschieht das ohne unsere Zustimmung und ist Betrug. Außerdem achten wir darauf, auf den Plattformen verifiziert zu sein. Wir würden sehr gern einen WhatsApp-Channel starten, aber Meta verifiziert uns dort nicht. Deshalb lassen wir es.

Die Scammer locken Menschen auf WhatsApp und dort findet der Betrug statt. Ohne ein klares Unterscheidungsmerkmal wie eine Verifizierung können wir dort nicht neben den Scammern existieren.

Gesellschaftlicher Schaden wiegt schwer

netzpolitik.org: Habt ihr gemerkt, ob die Aktionen geschäftsschädigend für euch wirken?

Thomas Kehl: Natürlich schadet es uns, wenn massenhaft Werbung auftaucht, die auf unserem Vertrauen aufbaut und dieses missbraucht. Das geht allen prominenten Personen so, denen so etwas passiert. Gerade im Finanzbereich geschieht das vielen, auch Journalisten oder Influencern. Eckart von Hirschhausens Autorität als Arzt wurde beispielsweise genutzt, um unseriöse Pillen zu verkaufen. Ich würde aber sagen, dass der gesellschaftliche Schaden höher ist als unser Schaden als Firma. Nichtsdestotrotz sind beides Gründe, dagegen vorzugehen.

Den Betroffenen aus unserem konkreten Fall haben wir unterstützt, so gut wir konnten. Er hat das auch verstanden und bereitwillig in unserem Video mitgewirkt, um über den Fall aufzuklären.

netzpolitik.org: Was wolltet ihr mit der Klage erreichen?

–––

Die Arbeit von netzpolitik.org finanziert sich aus den Spenden unserer Leser:innen. 
Unterstütze auch du unseren gemeinwohlorientierten, werbe- und trackingfreien Journalismus. Spende jetzt..

–––

Thomas Kehl: Wir haben uns zunächst aus zwei Gründen nur auf die Werbung konzentriert. Erstens hat sie eine viel größere Reichweite. Fake-Profile, die unsere Posts klauen, gibt es auch, aber gegen die kann man effizient vorgehen und sie haben kaum Reichweite. Zweitens verdient Meta mit der Werbung Geld. Deshalb lässt sich gut argumentieren, dass Meta auch dafür verantwortlich ist, welche Werbung sie verteilen. Meta sagt, das seien nicht ihre Inhalte und sie seien dafür nicht verantwortlich. Diesen Zahn hat das Gericht glücklicherweise gezogen: Meta hat die Anzeigen algorithmisch verteilt, und das genügt.

Andere sollen sich auf das Urteil berufen können

netzpolitik.org: Was bedeutet das Urteil jetzt weitergehend für Finanzfluss?

Thomas Kehl: Das Urteil ist noch nicht rechtskräftig. Meta hat einen Monat Zeit, Berufung einzulegen. Und davon ist auszugehen. Die nächste Instanz wäre das Oberlandesgericht Frankfurt. Darauf könnte der Bundesgerichtshof folgen. Wird das Urteil rechtskräftig, haftet Meta direkt für jede Anzeige mit meinem Bild oder mit Bezug zu Finanzfluss.

Bisher gilt der Notice-and-Take-Down-Mechanismus: Wir müssen jede Rechtsverletzung melden, und erst dann ist die Plattform verpflichtet, ihr nachzugehen. Das würde sich dann ändern. Wir könnten direkt auf Meta zugehen und sagen: Ihr habt hier eine Rechtsverletzung verursacht. Für jeden Verstoß gegen das Unterlassungsurteil könnten wir ein Ordnungsgeld von bis zu 250.000 Euro beantragen, das an die Staatskasse geht. Dazu kommt unser Schadensersatzanspruch.

Er bemisst sich an der Auskunft, die wir bekommen: wie oft die Anzeigen ausgespielt wurden und wie viel Geld Meta damit verdient hat. Dieses Geld steht Meta nicht zu, weil es mit rechtsverletzenden Inhalten verdient wurde. Wir sind die Inhaber der verwendeten Bilder. Uns ist klar, dass wir dieses Geld spenden würden, vermutlich für Verbraucherschutz. Wir wollen keinen Nutzen aus Betrug ziehen, so wie Meta das bisher gehandhabt hat.

netzpolitik.org: Wie schätzt ihr die weitergehende Bedeutung des Falles ein? Was könnte sich eurer Ansicht nach noch verbessern von Seiten Metas?

Thomas Kehl: Das Landgericht stützt sich auf eine sehr junge Rechtsprechung des Europäischen Gerichtshofs, der die Verantwortung von Plattformen gerade in diese Richtung entwickelt. Jetzt geht es darum, daraus nationale Präzedenzfälle zu machen.

Unser Wunsch ist, dass andere Betroffene sich auf dieses Urteil berufen können und nicht jeder bis zum Bundesgerichtshof gehen muss. Ich habe eine interessante Forderung gelesen und ich wundere mich, dass das noch nicht Pflicht ist. Wer bei Meta Werbung schaltet, sollte sich identifizieren müssen, so wie bei einer Kontoeröffnung. In Deutschland kann aktuell jeder ein Meta-Werbekonto eröffnen und Anzeigen schalten, ohne nachzuweisen, wer er ist. Dieser Forderung würde ich auf jeden Fall zustimmen.

netzpolitik.org: Ihr wünscht euch da also auch mehr Regulierung von Seiten der Politik, damit das nicht immer einzeln von Personen ausgefochten werden muss?

Thomas Kehl: Ja, definitiv.

–––

Deine Spende für digitale Freiheitsrechte 
Wir berichten über aktuelle netzpolitische Entwicklungen, decken Skandale auf und stoßen Debatten an. Dabei sind wir vollkommen unabhängig. Denn unser Kampf für digitale Freiheitsrechte finanziert sich aus den Spenden unserer Leser:innen. Jetzt spenden.

Meta hat uns ein sogenanntes Brand Protection Tool zur Verfügung gestellt, das überhaupt nicht protected. Manche Anzeigen wurden erst viele Tage nach der Meldung entfernt. In der Zwischenzeit fallen sehr viele Leute auf die Masche rein.

Teilweise wurden unsere Beschwerden auch abgelehnt und die Anzeigen verschwanden erst später.

–––

Gegen Ausweiskontrollen im Netz. 
Wir kämpfen für ein offenes Internet. Das geht nur mit deiner Unterstützung.

–––

netzpolitik.org: Wie war euer Umgang mit den Betroffenen?

Thomas Kehl: Wir haben jedem Betroffenen, der uns angeschrieben hat, empfohlen, Strafanzeige zu erstatten.

netzpolitik.org: Wie hoch sind die Schäden bei den Betroffe­nen?

Thomas Kehl: Wir haben mit einer Person gesprochen, die rund 50.000 Euro verloren hat. In der Summe lässt sich der Schaden nicht beziffern, die Dunkelziffer ist groß. Viele schämen sich, weil sie sich selbst für „so dumm“ halten, darauf hereingefallen zu sein. Ich würde das niemandem vorwerfen. Es ist nämlich nicht mehr diese plumpe Masche von früher. Heute wird das mit KI-generierten Videos und gefälschten Chats sehr professionell gemacht.

netzpolitik.org: Was war die Haltung der Geschädigten, als sie euch kontaktiert haben? Wie seid ihr damit umgegangen?

Thomas Kehl: Die Person, die 50.000 Euro verloren hat, hat mich auf LinkedIn angeschrieben, nachvollziehbarerweise ziemlich wütend. Sinngemäß: Wegen deiner Aktientipps bin ich ruiniert, wir müssen sprechen. Ich habe geantwortet: Das tut mir sehr leid, aber wir geben grundsätzlich keine Aktientipps. Danach schickte er mir Screenshots von WhatsApp-Chats mit „Thomas Kehl“. Da war schnell klar, dass Leute mich imitiert haben.

netzpolitik.org: Wie kann man wissen, wann es sich um Fake-Anzeigen oder ‑Profile handelt?

Thomas Kehl: Wir haben eine klare Regel für unsere Community: Wir schalten keine Werbung. Wenn irgendwo „Finanzfluss“-Werbung auftaucht, geschieht das ohne unsere Zustimmung und ist Betrug. Außerdem achten wir darauf, auf den Plattformen verifiziert zu sein. Wir würden sehr gern einen WhatsApp-Channel starten, aber Meta verifiziert uns dort nicht. Deshalb lassen wir es.

Die Scammer locken Menschen auf WhatsApp und dort findet der Betrug statt. Ohne ein klares Unterscheidungsmerkmal wie eine Verifizierung können wir dort nicht neben den Scammern existieren.

Gesellschaftlicher Schaden wiegt schwer

netzpolitik.org: Habt ihr gemerkt, ob die Aktionen geschäftsschädigend für euch wirken?

Thomas Kehl: Natürlich schadet es uns, wenn massenhaft Werbung auftaucht, die auf unserem Vertrauen aufbaut und dieses missbraucht. Das geht allen prominenten Personen so, denen so etwas passiert. Gerade im Finanzbereich geschieht das vielen, auch Journalisten oder Influencern. Eckart von Hirschhausens Autorität als Arzt wurde beispielsweise genutzt, um unseriöse Pillen zu verkaufen. Ich würde aber sagen, dass der gesellschaftliche Schaden höher ist als unser Schaden als Firma. Nichtsdestotrotz sind beides Gründe, dagegen vorzugehen.

Den Betroffenen aus unserem konkreten Fall haben wir unterstützt, so gut wir konnten. Er hat das auch verstanden und bereitwillig in unserem Video mitgewirkt, um über den Fall aufzuklären.

netzpolitik.org: Was wolltet ihr mit der Klage erreichen?

–––

Die Arbeit von netzpolitik.org finanziert sich aus den Spenden unserer Leser:innen. 
Unterstütze auch du unseren gemeinwohlorientierten, werbe- und trackingfreien Journalismus. Spende jetzt..

–––

Thomas Kehl: Wir haben uns zunächst aus zwei Gründen nur auf die Werbung konzentriert. Erstens hat sie eine viel größere Reichweite. Fake-Profile, die unsere Posts klauen, gibt es auch, aber gegen die kann man effizient vorgehen und sie haben kaum Reichweite. Zweitens verdient Meta mit der Werbung Geld. Deshalb lässt sich gut argumentieren, dass Meta auch dafür verantwortlich ist, welche Werbung sie verteilen. Meta sagt, das seien nicht ihre Inhalte und sie seien dafür nicht verantwortlich. Diesen Zahn hat das Gericht glücklicherweise gezogen: Meta hat die Anzeigen algorithmisch verteilt, und das genügt.

Andere sollen sich auf das Urteil berufen können

netzpolitik.org: Was bedeutet das Urteil jetzt weitergehend für Finanzfluss?

Thomas Kehl: Das Urteil ist noch nicht rechtskräftig. Meta hat einen Monat Zeit, Berufung einzulegen. Und davon ist auszugehen. Die nächste Instanz wäre das Oberlandesgericht Frankfurt. Darauf könnte der Bundesgerichtshof folgen. Wird das Urteil rechtskräftig, haftet Meta direkt für jede Anzeige mit meinem Bild oder mit Bezug zu Finanzfluss.

Bisher gilt der Notice-and-Take-Down-Mechanismus: Wir müssen jede Rechtsverletzung melden, und erst dann ist die Plattform verpflichtet, ihr nachzugehen. Das würde sich dann ändern. Wir könnten direkt auf Meta zugehen und sagen: Ihr habt hier eine Rechtsverletzung verursacht. Für jeden Verstoß gegen das Unterlassungsurteil könnten wir ein Ordnungsgeld von bis zu 250.000 Euro beantragen, das an die Staatskasse geht. Dazu kommt unser Schadensersatzanspruch.

Er bemisst sich an der Auskunft, die wir bekommen: wie oft die Anzeigen ausgespielt wurden und wie viel Geld Meta damit verdient hat. Dieses Geld steht Meta nicht zu, weil es mit rechtsverletzenden Inhalten verdient wurde. Wir sind die Inhaber der verwendeten Bilder. Uns ist klar, dass wir dieses Geld spenden würden, vermutlich für Verbraucherschutz. Wir wollen keinen Nutzen aus Betrug ziehen, so wie Meta das bisher gehandhabt hat.

netzpolitik.org: Wie schätzt ihr die weitergehende Bedeutung des Falles ein? Was könnte sich eurer Ansicht nach noch verbessern von Seiten Metas?

Thomas Kehl: Das Landgericht stützt sich auf eine sehr junge Rechtsprechung des Europäischen Gerichtshofs, der die Verantwortung von Plattformen gerade in diese Richtung entwickelt. Jetzt geht es darum, daraus nationale Präzedenzfälle zu machen.

Unser Wunsch ist, dass andere Betroffene sich auf dieses Urteil berufen können und nicht jeder bis zum Bundesgerichtshof gehen muss. Ich habe eine interessante Forderung gelesen und ich wundere mich, dass das noch nicht Pflicht ist. Wer bei Meta Werbung schaltet, sollte sich identifizieren müssen, so wie bei einer Kontoeröffnung. In Deutschland kann aktuell jeder ein Meta-Werbekonto eröffnen und Anzeigen schalten, ohne nachzuweisen, wer er ist. Dieser Forderung würde ich auf jeden Fall zustimmen.

netzpolitik.org: Ihr wünscht euch da also auch mehr Regulierung von Seiten der Politik, damit das nicht immer einzeln von Personen ausgefochten werden muss?

Thomas Kehl: Ja, definitiv.

–––

Deine Spende für digitale Freiheitsrechte 
Wir berichten über aktuelle netzpolitische Entwicklungen, decken Skandale auf und stoßen Debatten an. Dabei sind wir vollkommen unabhängig. Denn unser Kampf für digitale Freiheitsrechte finanziert sich aus den Spenden unserer Leser:innen. Jetzt spenden.

title: Beschlagnahme bei der ZEIT: Recherchematerial hat in Ermittlungen nichts zu suchen
subtitle: Bei der Durchsuchung von Redaktionen müssen alle Ampeln auf Rot springen. (Symbolbild) – Alle Rechte vorbehalten: IMAGO / Jürgen RitterDass …
feedText: Bei der Durchsuchung von Redaktionen müssen alle Ampeln auf Rot springen. (Symbolbild) – Alle Rechte vorbehalten: IMAGO / Jürgen RitterDass die Hamburger Polizei allen Ernstes Redaktionsräume der Zeit durchsuchen wollte, ist ein Frontalangriff auf die Pressefreiheit. Journalistisches Rohmaterial hat in den Händen von Staatsanwälten und Polizeien nichts verloren. Wenn wir das durchgehen lassen, erschüttern wir das Vertrauen in die Presse. Ein Kommentar.
articleBody:
Dass die Hamburger Polizei allen Ernstes Redaktionsräume der Zeit durchsuchen wollte, ist ein Frontalangriff auf die Pressefreiheit. Journalistisches Rohmaterial hat in den Händen von Staatsanwälten und Polizeien nichts verloren. Wenn wir das durchgehen lassen, erschüttern wir das Vertrauen in die Presse. Ein Kommentar.

Bei der Durchsuchung von Redaktionen müssen alle Ampeln auf Rot springen. (Symbolbild) – Alle Rechte vorbehalten: IMAGO / Jürgen Ritter
Wieder einmal hebeln Strafverfolgungsbehörden den Quellenschutz und damit die Pressefreiheit aus. Dieses Mal hat es „Die Zeit“ erwischt, bei der das Landeskriminalamt Hamburg und die Staatsanwaltschaft am Montag mit einem Durchsuchungsbeschluss für die Redaktion anrückte. Die Durchsuchung wehrte das Medium nur ab, weil es die fraglichen Daten freiwillig, „versiegelt“ und unter Widerspruch herausgab. Die Zeit protestiert gegen die Maßnahme, will den Durchsuchungsbeschluss anfechten und hofft darauf, dass die Daten vor einer gerichtlichen Entscheidung nicht genutzt werden.

Die Beschlagnahme von Interviewaufzeichnungen, also dem Rohmaterial eines Podcasts zum Block-Delling-Prozess beim Landgericht Hamburg, ist eine Frechheit. Der Schutz von Informant:innen und Quellen dient dazu, dass diese sich der Presse vertrauensvoll öffnen können, ohne Angst vor einer Enttarnung oder einer Verfolgung zu haben. Nur ein funktionierender Schutz der Quellen garantiert, dass die Presse ihre Aufgabe voll und ganz wahrnehmen kann.

Der Quellenschutz ist elementarer Bestandteil der Pressefreiheit – das ist auch höchstrichterlich mehrfach bestätigt worden. Grundsätzlich haben Journalist:innen ein umfassendes Zeugnisverweigerungsrecht, dazu kommt ein Beschlagnahmeverbot für Recherchematerial.

Pressefreiheit frontal angegriffen

Wer das, wie nun die Hamburger Ermittler, ignoriert, greift die Pressefreiheit frontal an. Das Bundesverfassungsgericht hat klargemacht, dass eine Durchsuchung in Redaktionsräumen nicht vorrangig dem Zweck dienen darf, den Verdacht von Straftaten durch Informanten aufzuklären – sondern dann schon die Pressevertreter:innen selbst beschuldigt sein müssen. Das ist bei der Zeit ausdrücklich nicht der Fall. Das Gericht will mit der Maßnahme neues Beweismaterial erheben und nebenbei die Glaubhaftigkeit der Zeugen überprüfen.

Wenn wir Staatsanwaltschaften, Polizeien und Gerichten solche Maßnahmen durchgehen lassen, erschüttern wir das Vertrauen in die Presse – und das schadet der Demokratie als Ganzes. Nur weil es sich beim Block-Prozess um ein Verfahren mit maximaler Medienaufmerksamkeit handelt, heißt das nicht, dass Polizei und Staatsanwaltschaft hier rechtsstaatliche Prinzipien mit Füßen treten dürfen.

–––

Die Arbeit von netzpolitik.org finanziert sich aus den Spenden unserer Leser:innen. 
Unterstütze auch du unseren gemeinwohlorientierten, werbe- und trackingfreien Journalismus. Spende jetzt..

–––

Es ist beileibe nicht das erste Mal, dass sich Staatsanwaltschaften an der Pressefreiheit vergehen. So ließ eine Staatsanwaltschaft 2013 gleich Wohnungen von fünf Fotografen durchsuchen, um an deren Bildmaterial zu kommen, mit dem ein Straftäter auf einer Demo identifiziert werden sollte. Im Jahr 2023 hatte die Polizei den Freiburger Sender Radio Dreyeckland und zwei Privatwohnungen durchsucht – die Maßnahme wurde jüngst vom Bundesverfassungsericht für rechtswidrig erklärt.

–––

Wir berichten über aktuelle netzpolitische Entwicklungen, decken Skandale auf und stoßen Debatten an. Dabei sind wir vollkommen unabhängig. Denn unser Kampf für digitale Freiheitsrechte finanziert sich aus den Spenden unserer Leser:innen. Jetzt spenden.

title: B. R. Ambedkar and the Dalit Quest for Dignity
subtitle: On the seventieth anniversary of Dr. B. R. Ambedkar’s mass conversion, a scholar reflects on the history and legacy of the Dalit Buddhist mo…
feedText:
On the seventieth anniversary of Dr. B. R. Ambedkar’s mass conversion, a scholar reflects on the history and legacy of the Dalit Buddhist movement.

The post B. R. Ambedkar and the Dalit Quest for Dignity appeared first on Tricycle: The Buddhist Review.
articleBody:
The value of a man was reduced to his immediate identity and nearest possibility. To a vote. To a number. To a thing. Never was a man treated as a mind. As a glorious thing made of star dust.

—Rohith Vemula, January 17, 2016

On a January morning in 2016, a 26-year-old PhD scholar at the University of Hyderabad left behind a suicide note that would shake India’s conscience. The Dalit student and activist Rohith Vemula had been suspended from his university, evicted from his hostel, and effectively erased from institutional life because of his caste and his activism with the Ambedkar Students’ Association (ASA). His words have since become one of the most quoted testimonies to the lived reality of caste in modern India.

Rohith’s death did not silence his family. Three months later, on April 14, 2016—the 125th birth anniversary of Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, the famed Dalit activist and chief architect of the Indian Constitution—his mother, Radhika, and his brother, Raja, traveled from Hyderabad to the Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar Bhavan in Dadar, Mumbai, where thirty Buddhist monks administered the Deeksha vows in the presence of Prakash Ambedkar, the great man’s grandson. They converted to Buddhism. Rohith’s childhood friend Riyaz Shaikh and ASA activist Charbad Raju converted alongside them.

They convert to Buddhism as protest, as survival, as the most radical act available to them: the refusal to remain within a religion that sanctifies their humiliation.

This act of conversion in response to violence is neither new nor isolated in India. It is a pattern woven through seven decades of Ambedkarite history: Caste commits violence, the state fails to respond, and Dalits reach not for weapons but for the dhamma. They convert to Buddhism as protest, as survival, as the most radical act available to them: the refusal to remain within a religion that sanctifies their humiliation.

The World Ambedkar Inherited

To understand why Dalits convert to Buddhism when atrocities occur, one must first understand what they are converting from. Caste is not merely social stratification; it is a theological architecture of pollution and purity, inscribed in shastras (scripture), enforced through violence, and reproduced across generations. For those designated “untouchable”—outside the fourfold varna system entirely—it meant being prohibited from access to temples, wells, schools, transport, jobs, and roads. It meant being forced to announce one’s presence by striking two stones together so caste Hindus could step aside. It meant sweeping streets, carrying human waste, skinning dead cattle—not by choice but by birth. It meant that one’s very shadow was considered contaminating.

Dr. Ambedkar was born into this reality on April 14, 1891. A brilliant student who earned doctorates from Columbia University and the London School of Economics, he was nonetheless barred from drinking water from a common pot in his own school, denied accommodation by landlords, and turned away from guesthouses throughout his professional life. He understood that no amount of personal achievement could dissolve caste as long as Hinduism provided its theological justification. His conclusion, reached after decades of study, political struggle, and searching engagement with multiple religious traditions, was unambiguous: Hinduism and caste were inseparable. Reform from within was impossible. Liberation required exit.

The Dhamma Deeksha: Ambedkar’s Mass Conversion

On October 14, 1956, in the city of Nagpur, in the year of the celebration of the 2,500th anniversary of the Buddha’s passage into parinirvana, Dr. Ambedkar led approximately 500,000 followers in a mass conversion to Buddhism—what became known as the Dhamma Deeksha. He was 64, gravely ill, and knew he was dying. (He died in his sleep six weeks later, three days after completing The Buddha and His Dhamma, which would become the foundational text for the Ambedkarite movement.) Before his death, he was determined to set a new school of engaged Buddhism in motion—what he termed Navayana, or the “New Vehicle.”

In taking the twenty-two vows Ambedkar prescribed, new Buddhists simultaneously rejected Hindu gods, the authority of Brahminical priests, the legitimacy of caste, and the identity of untouchability itself. They were not joining a religion so much as declaring their humanity. The vows made this explicit: “I renounce Hinduism, which is harmful for humanity and impedes the advancement of human beings, and I embrace Buddhism as my religion,” and “I believe that today I am taking new birth.” This language of rebirth was chosen with care. Buddhism offered not just a new faith but a new identity—one whose dignity was not contingent on caste, whose spiritual worth was not determined by birth, whose liberation was possible here, in this world, through ethical engagement. Further, in their explicit refusal to worship Hindu deities and to view the Buddha as an avatar of the Hindu god Vishnu, the vows push back against Hindu nationalist attempts to absorb Buddhism back into Hinduism and therefore weaken Buddhism’s power to challenge caste. Taken together, these twenty-two vows laid the foundation for Ambedkarite Buddhism, which offered a fierce rejection of Hindu nationalism and caste politics while affirming the inherent dignity and equality of all beings.

Taken together, these twenty-two vows laid the foundation for Ambedkarite Buddhism, which offered a fierce rejection of Hindu nationalism and caste politics while affirming the inherent dignity and equality of all beings. 

In laying out the tenets of the Navayana movement, Ambedkar did not present the Buddha as a god to worship but as Margadata—one who shows the path. The dhamma, he insisted in The Buddha and His Dhamma, served as a social blueprint: “The function of Dhamma is to reconstruct the world.” He drew from the Pali canon’s democratic sangha as model for egalitarian community, from the Mahayana’s bodhisattva ideal as model for social service, and from his analysis of Indian society to reframe dukkha not as cosmic suffering but as the specific, structural suffering imposed by caste.

Ambedkar timed the Dhamma Deeksha to take place on the date of the Emperor Ashoka’s conversion to Buddhism. But when Emperor Ashoka converted to Buddhism in the 3rd century BCE, the conversion “came from the throne.” Imperial patronage supported monasteries and spread the dhamma throughout Asia. Ambedkar’s revival, by contrast, “came from the people”—specifically from those deemed to occupy the lowest stratum of society. This origin from the very bottom of India’s social hierarchy fundamentally shapes Ambedkarite Buddhism and explains why it carries such a sense of moral urgency. What Ambedkar left behind was not merely a new Buddhism but a new form of resistance—one that subsequent generations of Dalits would turn to whenever the violence of caste made remaining inside Hinduism unbearable.

Buddhists gather in Nagpur in 2006 to celebrate the fiftieth Anniversary of Ambedkar’s Buddhist conversion. Photo by Shashi Jambhulkar. Courtesy Santosh Raut.

Ambedkar’s Legacy

In the seventy years since that October morning in Nagpur, the pattern of caste violence has repeated with devastating regularity. Caste commits atrocities, and the state looks away. And Dalits, following in Ambedkar’s footsteps, respond by converting to Buddhism—not in defeat but in defiance.

In July 2016, four young Dalit men from Mota Samadhiyala village near Una, Gujarat, were stripped, bound to an SUV, and flogged publicly by cow vigilantes. Their crime was skinning a dead cow, the traditional occupation their caste had been assigned for centuries. Their attackers filmed the assault and circulated the footage. The police, presented with video evidence, were slow to act. The victims and hundreds of their family members embraced Buddhism in protest: If Hinduism made them responsible for dead cows and then targeted them for doing so, they would leave Hinduism. The act of conversion was at once a rejection of the theological framework that assigned them this labor and an assertion of dignity in the face of violence and humiliation.

In 2019, in Gundlupet, a Dalit youth was stripped, thrashed, and paraded naked—an act of humiliation designed to communicate to an entire community their assigned place. Dalit activists organized protest marches that concluded with several individuals converting to Buddhism. The symbolism was significant: In response to an act of forced stripping, these Dalits voluntarily adopted a tradition that strips a person of their caste identity at the moment of conversion.

In 2022, two Dalit youths in Bhulon Village were assaulted by upper-caste men for the act of offering aarti (prayer) at a Hindu temple—a devotional practice considered the prerogative of caste Hindus. The police refused to file cases against the offenders. More than 200 Dalit families converted to Buddhism collectively in protest, as Buddhism offered them a house of worship where no upper-caste gatekeeper could deny them entry.

Some conversions are not singular events but the culmination of long struggles. The Namantar Andolan—the sixteen-year movement to rename Marathwada University after Dr. Ambedkar—was marked by sustained upper-caste violence: riots, murders, destruction of Dalit property, burning of homes. Dominant castes attacked the very proposal of honoring Ambedkar with an institution bearing his name. But the violence did not suppress the Dalit Buddhist movement. After nearly two decades of advocacy, the university was eventually renamed in 1994, but what the struggle solidified was more enduring: a Buddhist identity in the region inseparable from political resistance.

Buddhists celebrate the fiftieth anniversary of Ambedkar’s Buddhist conversion. Photo by Shashi Jambhulkar. Courtesy Santosh Raut.

Rohith Vemula: A Life Reduced to a Number

No case has more powerfully illustrated the intersection of caste, institutional violence, and Buddhist response than that of Rohith Vemula. Rohith was an activist with the Ambedkar Students’ Association at the University of Hyderabad. Following a political clash with a right-wing student group, the university administration suspended him and four other Dalit student leaders, evicting them from their hostel and banning them from common spaces. They lived in a makeshift tent on campus. On January 17, 2016, Rohith committed suicide.

His suicide note is not a document of despair alone. It is a philosophical protest—a young man who dreamed of stars and galaxies articulating what the caste system does to the inner life of a human being. The phrase “My birth is a fatal accident” does not describe personal misfortune. It describes a social system in which being born in a particular caste is a life sentence. His note ends: “From shadows to the stars.”

His family understood. His body was cremated according to Buddhist rites. Three months later, on Ambedkar Jayanti, his mother and brother converted to Buddhism in Mumbai, taking the Deeksha vows. “From today,” Raja Vemula stated, “my mother and I will be free from shame, free from the daily humiliation, free from the guilt of praying to the same god in whose name our people have been tortured for centuries. . . . We want azadi [freedom] from the caste system.” Rohith had urged his family toward Buddhism while he was alive. In death, he finally brought them there.

A New Buddhism Born from Old Symbols

What is being created through these conversions is not simply a transfer of religious allegiance. It is the emergence of a distinctly Ambedkarite Buddhist culture rooted in the particular experience of caste. In Buddhist viharas across Maharashtra, the altar holds two images: the meditating Buddha and Dr. Ambedkar in his characteristic blue suit with pen, holding the Constitution he helped to craft. The pairing is deliberate: One offers the path; the other shows how that path was walked in modernity.

Sunday weekly dhamma class at the Sariputta Buddhist Vihara in Nagpur. Photo by Shashi Jambhulkar. Courtesy Santosh Raut.

Ancient Buddhist symbols are being reimagined through Ambedkarite imagination: The dharmachakra appears on protest banners alongside photographs of atrocity victims; the blue of Ambedkar’s suit has become the color of Dalit assertion; the Bodhi tree is reclaimed as a symbol of enlightenment available to all, not just the ritually pure. Conversion ceremonies are conducted on Ambedkar Jayanti and Dhamma Chakra Pravartan Din to connect each individual act to the collective history of 1956. At local viharas, monks and laypeople administer the twenty-two vows together, dissolving the hierarchies that traditionally separated clergy from laity. In Rohith’s case, even death became a Buddhist ritual act—his cremation insisting that his mind, “a glorious thing made of star dust,” was never reducible to his caste.

Participants engage in metta bhavana meditation at the Dhammakranti Retreat in Nagpur in 2006. Photo by Shashi Jambhulkar. Courtesy Santosh Raut.

From Shadows to the Stars

When Rohith Vemula signed his final letter, “From shadows to the stars,” he was thinking of Carl Sagan and the cosmos. But the phrase has taken on a meaning larger than one man’s biography. It has become an Ambedkarite phrase, describing the journey from the shadow of caste to the light of Buddhist liberation, from the imposed darkness of untouchability to the possibility of human dignity.

Ambedkar understood this journey. “The greatest thing that the Buddha has done,” he wrote, “is to tell the world that the world cannot be reformed except by the reformation of the mind of the man and the mind of the world.” Spiritual revolution becomes the foundation for social transformation. This is what conversion enacts: a reformation of mind, a refusal to carry within oneself the shame that caste assigns. It is what Raja Vemula was describing when he said his family would be free from shame. Shame is structured into the caste system. Buddhism, in the Ambedkarite tradition, dismantles it.

For 10 million Ambedkarite Buddhists, the dhamma provides the moral foundation enabling constitutional democracy to flourish. In Ambedkar’s formulation, the Buddhist principle of maitri (loving-kindness) becomes the democratic principle of fraternity. Anatta (not-self) provides the basis for constitutional equality, as caste hierarchy is revealed to be an illusion. And the Pali canon’s descriptions of sangha become the model for democratic governance and community. But the answer is also the people themselves. When they march with Buddhist flags instead of weapons, when they demand justice with dignity, when they build communities of equality in a hierarchical society, they are collectively enacting the vision of Ambedkar’s Constitution, enabling it to flourish.

Participants celebrate the fiftieth anniversary of Ambedkar’s conversion. Photo by Shashi Jambhulkar. Courtesy Santosh Raut.

Seventy years after Ambedkar’s conversion, his movement stands at a crossroads determining not only its own future but potentially the future of engaged Buddhism globally. The challenges it faces offer a template for how Buddhism can meet the social challenges of the modern age and set forth a path of liberation not just for individuals seeking peace but for communities seeking justice. For the global Buddhist community, Ambedkarite Buddhism poses an uncomfortable but necessary question: Can we learn from Buddhists who are actually transforming society, or will we continue ignoring them?

When we speak of engaged Buddhism, remember that 10 million people are already doing it, not as a theoretical concept but as lived reality, carrying within their bodies the memory of every flogging, every temple door slammed shut, every act of institutional violence, and choosing, still, the path of peace. The question is whether the rest of us are watching silently—or paying attention and ready to join in.

Ambedkar timed the Dhamma Deeksha to take place on the date of the Emperor Ashoka’s conversion to Buddhism. But when Emperor Ashoka converted to Buddhism in the 3rd century BCE, the conversion “came from the throne.” Imperial patronage supported monasteries and spread the dhamma throughout Asia. Ambedkar’s revival, by contrast, “came from the people”—specifically from those deemed to occupy the lowest stratum of society. This origin from the very bottom of India’s social hierarchy fundamentally shapes Ambedkarite Buddhism and explains why it carries such a sense of moral urgency. What Ambedkar left behind was not merely a new Buddhism but a new form of resistance—one that subsequent generations of Dalits would turn to whenever the violence of caste made remaining inside Hinduism unbearable.

Buddhists gather in Nagpur in 2006 to celebrate the fiftieth Anniversary of Ambedkar’s Buddhist conversion. Photo by Shashi Jambhulkar. Courtesy Santosh Raut.

Ambedkar’s Legacy

In the seventy years since that October morning in Nagpur, the pattern of caste violence has repeated with devastating regularity. Caste commits atrocities, and the state looks away. And Dalits, following in Ambedkar’s footsteps, respond by converting to Buddhism—not in defeat but in defiance.

In July 2016, four young Dalit men from Mota Samadhiyala village near Una, Gujarat, were stripped, bound to an SUV, and flogged publicly by cow vigilantes. Their crime was skinning a dead cow, the traditional occupation their caste had been assigned for centuries. Their attackers filmed the assault and circulated the footage. The police, presented with video evidence, were slow to act. The victims and hundreds of their family members embraced Buddhism in protest: If Hinduism made them responsible for dead cows and then targeted them for doing so, they would leave Hinduism. The act of conversion was at once a rejection of the theological framework that assigned them this labor and an assertion of dignity in the face of violence and humiliation.

In 2019, in Gundlupet, a Dalit youth was stripped, thrashed, and paraded naked—an act of humiliation designed to communicate to an entire community their assigned place. Dalit activists organized protest marches that concluded with several individuals converting to Buddhism. The symbolism was significant: In response to an act of forced stripping, these Dalits voluntarily adopted a tradition that strips a person of their caste identity at the moment of conversion.

In 2022, two Dalit youths in Bhulon Village were assaulted by upper-caste men for the act of offering aarti (prayer) at a Hindu temple—a devotional practice considered the prerogative of caste Hindus. The police refused to file cases against the offenders. More than 200 Dalit families converted to Buddhism collectively in protest, as Buddhism offered them a house of worship where no upper-caste gatekeeper could deny them entry.

Some conversions are not singular events but the culmination of long struggles. The Namantar Andolan—the sixteen-year movement to rename Marathwada University after Dr. Ambedkar—was marked by sustained upper-caste violence: riots, murders, destruction of Dalit property, burning of homes. Dominant castes attacked the very proposal of honoring Ambedkar with an institution bearing his name. But the violence did not suppress the Dalit Buddhist movement. After nearly two decades of advocacy, the university was eventually renamed in 1994, but what the struggle solidified was more enduring: a Buddhist identity in the region inseparable from political resistance.

Buddhists celebrate the fiftieth anniversary of Ambedkar’s Buddhist conversion. Photo by Shashi Jambhulkar. Courtesy Santosh Raut.

Rohith Vemula: A Life Reduced to a Number

No case has more powerfully illustrated the intersection of caste, institutional violence, and Buddhist response than that of Rohith Vemula. Rohith was an activist with the Ambedkar Students’ Association at the University of Hyderabad. Following a political clash with a right-wing student group, the university administration suspended him and four other Dalit student leaders, evicting them from their hostel and banning them from common spaces. They lived in a makeshift tent on campus. On January 17, 2016, Rohith committed suicide.

His suicide note is not a document of despair alone. It is a philosophical protest—a young man who dreamed of stars and galaxies articulating what the caste system does to the inner life of a human being. The phrase “My birth is a fatal accident” does not describe personal misfortune. It describes a social system in which being born in a particular caste is a life sentence. His note ends: “From shadows to the stars.”

His family understood. His body was cremated according to Buddhist rites. Three months later, on Ambedkar Jayanti, his mother and brother converted to Buddhism in Mumbai, taking the Deeksha vows. “From today,” Raja Vemula stated, “my mother and I will be free from shame, free from the daily humiliation, free from the guilt of praying to the same god in whose name our people have been tortured for centuries. . . . We want azadi [freedom] from the caste system.” Rohith had urged his family toward Buddhism while he was alive. In death, he finally brought them there.

A New Buddhism Born from Old Symbols

What is being created through these conversions is not simply a transfer of religious allegiance. It is the emergence of a distinctly Ambedkarite Buddhist culture rooted in the particular experience of caste. In Buddhist viharas across Maharashtra, the altar holds two images: the meditating Buddha and Dr. Ambedkar in his characteristic blue suit with pen, holding the Constitution he helped to craft. The pairing is deliberate: One offers the path; the other shows how that path was walked in modernity.

Sunday weekly dhamma class at the Sariputta Buddhist Vihara in Nagpur. Photo by Shashi Jambhulkar. Courtesy Santosh Raut.

Ancient Buddhist symbols are being reimagined through Ambedkarite imagination: The dharmachakra appears on protest banners alongside photographs of atrocity victims; the blue of Ambedkar’s suit has become the color of Dalit assertion; the Bodhi tree is reclaimed as a symbol of enlightenment available to all, not just the ritually pure. Conversion ceremonies are conducted on Ambedkar Jayanti and Dhamma Chakra Pravartan Din to connect each individual act to the collective history of 1956. At local viharas, monks and laypeople administer the twenty-two vows together, dissolving the hierarchies that traditionally separated clergy from laity. In Rohith’s case, even death became a Buddhist ritual act—his cremation insisting that his mind, “a glorious thing made of star dust,” was never reducible to his caste.

Participants engage in metta bhavana meditation at the Dhammakranti Retreat in Nagpur in 2006. Photo by Shashi Jambhulkar. Courtesy Santosh Raut.

From Shadows to the Stars

When Rohith Vemula signed his final letter, “From shadows to the stars,” he was thinking of Carl Sagan and the cosmos. But the phrase has taken on a meaning larger than one man’s biography. It has become an Ambedkarite phrase, describing the journey from the shadow of caste to the light of Buddhist liberation, from the imposed darkness of untouchability to the possibility of human dignity.

Ambedkar understood this journey. “The greatest thing that the Buddha has done,” he wrote, “is to tell the world that the world cannot be reformed except by the reformation of the mind of the man and the mind of the world.” Spiritual revolution becomes the foundation for social transformation. This is what conversion enacts: a reformation of mind, a refusal to carry within oneself the shame that caste assigns. It is what Raja Vemula was describing when he said his family would be free from shame. Shame is structured into the caste system. Buddhism, in the Ambedkarite tradition, dismantles it.

For 10 million Ambedkarite Buddhists, the dhamma provides the moral foundation enabling constitutional democracy to flourish. In Ambedkar’s formulation, the Buddhist principle of maitri (loving-kindness) becomes the democratic principle of fraternity. Anatta (not-self) provides the basis for constitutional equality, as caste hierarchy is revealed to be an illusion. And the Pali canon’s descriptions of sangha become the model for democratic governance and community. But the answer is also the people themselves. When they march with Buddhist flags instead of weapons, when they demand justice with dignity, when they build communities of equality in a hierarchical society, they are collectively enacting the vision of Ambedkar’s Constitution, enabling it to flourish.

Participants celebrate the fiftieth anniversary of Ambedkar’s conversion. Photo by Shashi Jambhulkar. Courtesy Santosh Raut.

Seventy years after Ambedkar’s conversion, his movement stands at a crossroads determining not only its own future but potentially the future of engaged Buddhism globally. The challenges it faces offer a template for how Buddhism can meet the social challenges of the modern age and set forth a path of liberation not just for individuals seeking peace but for communities seeking justice. For the global Buddhist community, Ambedkarite Buddhism poses an uncomfortable but necessary question: Can we learn from Buddhists who are actually transforming society, or will we continue ignoring them?

When we speak of engaged Buddhism, remember that 10 million people are already doing it, not as a theoretical concept but as lived reality, carrying within their bodies the memory of every flogging, every temple door slammed shut, every act of institutional violence, and choosing, still, the path of peace. The question is whether the rest of us are watching silently—or paying attention and ready to join in.

title: Contemplations on the Five Mindfulness Trainings
subtitle: Two dharma teachers in the Plum Village tradition on how the precepts can help us lead ethical lives in the face of injustice and oppression…
feedText:
Two dharma teachers in the Plum Village tradition on how the precepts can help us lead ethical lives in the face of injustice and oppression

The post Contemplations on the Five Mindfulness Trainings appeared first on Tricycle: The Buddhist Review.
articleBody:
Grief and love are deeply interconnected, and it was my experience of both that led me to write the article “Contemplations on the Five Mindfulness Trainings: A New Paradigm for Racial Justice and the Global Pandemic.” I began writing in 2019 as I supported my brother, Sam, month after month during his treatment for chronic heart failure, which eventually led to his death in February 2020. I was not only grieving his death, but I was also mourning the end of my ambiguous and complicated fifteen-year marriage. This was followed by desperate months of quarantine, isolation, and physical distance due to the Covid pandemic. Each day revealed new and disturbing information about the disproportionate impact of Covid on Black and Latinx people, immigrants, and low-income communities. And then came the police killings of George Floyd, Breonna Taylor, and others; the worldwide and national protests calling to defund the police; and the expansion of the Black Lives Matter movement. As each event cascaded into the next, I knew instinctively to turn to the Plum Village mindfulness practice and teachings.

Months before, I had visited Blue Cliff Monastery, a mindfulness practice center in the Plum Village lineage in upstate New York. Just as I was about to walk to the front of the Great Togetherness Hall to offer a dharma talk, a nun had approached me and given me a copy of the Sutra on Transforming Violence and Fear. I turned to this sutra to help me understand my own feelings and the colliding events within the United States and beyond. I read and reflected on the sutra almost daily. Then I began reading the Third Mindfulness Training on True Love because love seemed distant and inaccessible, especially in light of my divorce. Each day, line by line, I read and reflected on this Training and this sutra in the presence of my brother’s death, the global pandemic, and the social upheaval happening all around me.

Shortly after my brother died, protests for racial justice in the United States spread rapidly, with calls for a worldwide reckoning on race in the United States and other countries, I participated in a two-hour virtual healing gathering for BIPOC, led by Ruth King, a respected teacher in the Theravada tradition and author of Mindful of Race: Transforming Racism from the Inside Out. It was sponsored by Liberate (now called The Village), a mindfulness app designed for BIPOC. Hundreds of people gathered, expressing grief, rage, and anger. I felt confusion and anger in me as I listened to the speakers. And then Ruth King asked a life-changing question: How do you fight injustice without hating?

Ruth King asked a life-changing question: How do you fight injustice without hating?

The question became a bell of mindfulness for me. I continued to read and reflect on the sutra, the Third Mindfulness Training, and this powerful question. I began to think deeply about the meaning of power, power dynamics, and how to offer my power more skillfully and in greater service to others. Interestingly, my dharma name is Chan Tang Luc—True Sangha Power, or True Power of the Sangha. A dharma name is a personalized name given by a teacher to a student upon their ordination or taking precepts, symbolizing the practitioner’s unique spiritual path. After I received this name at the Fourteen Mindfulness Trainings ordination ceremony in 2003, Sister Chân Đức approached me and said, “Power is not what you think it is.” That stayed with me. I have come to understand that she was referring to the Five Spiritual Powers that Thích Nhất Hạnh articulated in his book The Art of Power: faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and insight.

With all this in mind, the Contemplations on the Five Mindfulness Trainings emerged. I was motivated to write them to understand and make sense of my feelings of numbness, loss, and grief, as well as my outrage over the social upheaval occurring at that time. I spoke to Marisela Gomez, a dear friend and mindfulness practitioner who is now a lay dharma teacher, and we agreed to write an article. The last time we had written an essay together was in 2015, after a white supremacist murdered nine Black worshippers at the historic Emanuel African Methodist Episcopal Church in Charleston, South Carolina. We wrote that essay to better understand our feelings, as a path of self-healing and self-love, and to offer love and support to others who were feeling rage, terror, and so much more.

Sometimes to truly heal from loss and grief, we need to come face to face with a difficult truth, with regret, pain, and old wounds that are asking for a second chance to be lifted up, woven back into our life, cherished, and welcomed home. At times, my life has felt like a long process of coming to terms with a series of losses that led me to seek inner healing and inner peace. In a roundabout way, I was being invited toward forgiveness, peacemaking, and compassionate action, to live and love in the direction of kindness and vulnerability. Yet a period of profound personal losses combined with the events of the time brought me to a place of tender fragility, fear, and anxiety. I leaned on my many friends and family members—and still do.

I was especially supported in this healing process by reciting the Five Mindfulness Trainings, sometimes called the Five Wonderful Precepts, as well as the Fourteen Mindfulness Trainings of the Plum Village tradition founded by Zen Master Thích Nhất Hạnh. These Trainings, which I also refer to as precepts, were offered by the Buddha to his monastic and lay followers as clear guidance to lead an ethical, mindful, and joyful life. Thích Nhất Hạnh has described these precepts in countless books and worldwide teachings as a way to cultivate a peaceful and harmonious life.

The Five Mindfulness Trainings help us answer pivotal life questions:

How should I live?
What energy do I want to bring when I enter a room?
How do I act under the circumstances?
What inner guidance informs my behavior?
What are my values?
What is the world asking of me?

Our individual responses to these questions are shaped by our life experience, our values, and sometimes by our energy, health and well-being, and so much more. Whether we are aware of them or not, each of us probably already lives by a set of precepts, or principles and values. Many of us are guided by common precepts such as truthfulness, honesty, and refraining from stealing and cheating. From a tender age, we are taught these ways of becoming “good citizens” in the world, in the workplace, in our family, and with ourselves.

Some people take these precepts through formal vows, such as codes of school or religious conduct. For many, though, these vows can become wooden, flat, perfunctory, and then forgotten over time. We “set and forget” them and then feel bereft from inner guidance when we most need it. So how do we bring these precepts, this internal guidance system, into our daily life and call on them when we need them the most?

Over the years, in attending retreats with Thầy and the Plum Village community, I have come to understand that the precepts are not linear. Instead, each precept connects and is interdependent with all of the precepts. For example, the first precept on reverence for life is interdependent with the fifth precept on consuming mindfully. Since they are all interwoven, practicing one precept will impact your practice of the others. Not only are the precepts interconnected, but we are also interconnected to each other and all the elements in the cosmos. Because of all this, and because our actions have an impact on others whether we are aware of it or not, when you practice the precepts, you are not doing so for yourself alone, as a separate entity—you are doing so for all beings. What you consume and how you consume will have an impact on yourself, on others, and on the earth.

According to Thầy’s teachings on emptiness, your body isn’t just yours; your body belongs to your parents, society, and future generations. All of these have come together to manifest your body, including the trees, the clouds, and the oceans. Your body and your practice are manifestations of the whole cosmos. To practice the precepts is to support not only yourself but also your ancestors, your parents, future generations, and society. To practice the precepts is to recognize this interdependent relationship between you and the cosmos. The precepts are about cultivating conscious awareness and connectedness, especially now, in a society that has gone numb with divisiveness, too-muchness, and too-fastness.

The precepts are an invitation to be in touch with what is wholesome and beneficial in and around us. They are bells of mindfulness. Ultimately, the precepts are opportunities to live and grow a compassionate life of love, peace, and understanding. We might be challenged in our practice at times, and at those times we need to recommit ourselves and reconnect with spiritual friends who support us on the path toward living a healthy and wholesome life.

–Valerie Brown

Contemplations on the Five Mindfulness Trainings

Preamble to the Contemplations on the Five Mindfulness Trainings

Let us open to another way of understanding the Five Mindfulness Trainings, guiding principles for mindful and ethical living, which call us toward individual and collective awakening, compassion, and peace. We are interconnected. What happens in one part of the universe affects people everywhere. What happens to the Black body affects all bodies. We are called forward. Global pandemics, the climate crisis, social and economic oppression and upheaval are gateways to suffering worldwide, disproportionately impacting Black, Indigenous, and other people of color; disabled people; people currently and historically subject to poverty, war, and genocide; LGBTQIA+ people; people facing health inequities and premature death; people facing generational displacement; and people with historically socially marginalized identities, including those facing oppression because of their abilities, gender, or immigration status. They, we, are not alone. Our lives and livelihoods are interconnected. We are called forward.

We cannot exist independent of, for example, low-wage workers, health care workers, unhoused people, single mothers, undocumented people, the unemployed and underemployed, and similarly situated people. If one such person lives on the knife edge of racial, ethnic, social, structural, and systemic oppression and discrimination, we are all affected. We are called forward.

The practitioner dwells in the now, recognizing the dualistic nature of equanimity and instability, discrimination and nondiscrimination, ill-being and well-being. We practice right view and compassionate action, moving toward right insight. Aware of the interconnectedness and interdependence of all life, we courageously turn to practice wholeheartedly. We are called forward.

Lighting a stick of incense, listening to the sutras, sitting upright and solid, palms joined, the practitioner looks within, and in concentration the path and fruit of skillful action are revealed. We are called forward.

Speak aloud these words with the sangha voice, a true river of understanding.

Contemplation on the First Mindfulness Training: Acknowledging Beauty as Reverence for Life

Aware of the suffering caused by oppression and generational harm based on racial, cultural, social, and ethnic inferiority and superiority, I acknowledge the beauty and violence inherent in life. I vow to resist being complicit in systems and structures that continue to perpetuate injustice, violence, hatred, and delusion instead of reverence of life for marginalized groups and others. I recognize that each person contributes to my individual and our collective awakening, and to the co-creation of a world that celebrates and affirms differences and similarities. All living beings can teach me something, when I remember to pause, breathe, listen deeply with a calm and open mind and heart, and ask myself, “Is there more?” or “What else is here with me?” I honor and respect all life, guided by right view and right effort.

Contemplation on the Second Mindfulness Training: Belonging and Connecting as True Happiness

Aware of the suffering caused by ignorance and aversion of my own and others’ racial, ethnic, cultural, and social history, its legacy and how this affects me, I am committed to learning and connecting to these histories. Aware that there is no genetic or biological difference among racial and ethnic groups, and that these identities were socially constructed by one group to establish dominance over others, I will turn toward all forms of othering with the aspiration of transforming heart and mind. I know that this history has led to fragmentation inside and outside the body and mind and has brought much suffering to all beings. I will notice when emotions of belonging and othering arise, and I will ask myself, “Why?” Whatever feelings, perceptions, or mental formations arise in me, I will embrace and engage them with love in action. I am committed to practicing right resolve, right speech, right action, and right livelihood so I can help relieve this legacy of racial and social suffering. I will practice looking deeply to see that true happiness is not possible without true connection leading to belonging and understanding.

Contemplation on the Third Mindfulness Training: Cherishment as True Love

Aware of the suffering caused by discrimination and oppression, I vow to transform these seeds in myself, my sangha, and society. I recognize the ways in which I have benefitted or not benefitted, explicitly or implicitly, from systems and structures of injustice. I am aware of the legacy of violence, including unlawful police violence, perpetrated against people of various gender identities, expressions, and sexual orientations, Black people, indigenous people, people of color, disabled people, undocumented people, people suffering mental health challenges, and others who are marginalized. I am committed to looking tenderly at my suffering, knowing that I am not separate from others and that the seeds of suffering contain the seeds of joy. I am aware that narrow interpretations of intimate relationships constrain how we cherish each other in our expression of love, leaving many isolated and alienated. I am not afraid of bold love that fosters compassion, justice, and peace, and tender love that seeks understanding. I cherish this breath, body, mind, and moment as an act of healing for myself and for others. I cherish the liberation of all beings guided by the wisdom and the solidity of the sangha as my path of true love.

Contemplation on the Fourth Mindfulness Training: Vulnerability as Deep Listening and Loving Speech

Aware that vulnerability is the essence of our true nature, our humanness, I vow to risk listening for understanding rather than disagreement. I am committed to generous and courageous listening that bridges differences and supports others who may be different from me. When I am not able to understand others, I vow to come back to my breath and my body, and to offer myself gentle patience. I am aware that loving communication rests on honesty, compassion, and openness that align with my highest aspiration to alleviate suffering. When I have hurt others through my unskillful listening or speech, I vow to practice true beneficial regret, making a good apology that acknowledges what I have done and the harm caused, accepting responsibility and being accountable for my behavior, and offering sincere regret for my actions, knowing that this supports the other person and me. Through my practices of vulnerability, forgiveness, and deep listening, I know that my speech will be guided by love and understanding. Practicing in this way supports right speech and right action and guides me to right insight.

Contemplation on the Fifth Mindfulness Training: Welcoming as True Nourishing and Healing

Aware of the suffering caused by the consumption of an inadequate history of racial and ethnic forms of social segregation and injustice, I am committed to healing myself and the world. I am aware that my thoughts, perceptions, feelings, words, and actions may have been influenced by this history. I vow to understand how I have been influenced by embracing and denying this racial, social, and ethnic history of inferiority, superiority, and equality. I will cultivate joy to nourish me in this aspiration. I will practice mindfulness of the four kinds of nutriments to become aware of how edible foods, sense impressions, volition, and consciousness are all influenced by this history. Practicing with right energy and right resolve, my conscious consumption will be guided by right action that welcomes differences without discrimination. This right insight offers true welcoming on this path to nourish and heal myself, my ancestors, my descendants, my sangha, and society.

The Five Mindfulness Trainings keep us centered in life’s storms and joys and remind us that life is a precious gift. The Trainings are a path to liberation and transformation. Practicing these Trainings supports us toward racial and ethnic reconciliation and social change and heals deep suffering. The Five Mindfulness Trainings help us cross this shore of suffering and bring us to the side of true awakening and love. The Contemplations on the Five Mindfulness Trainings are a commentary to these foundational teachings and are meant to offer another way of understanding Thich Nhất Hạnh’s teachings to live an ethical life. We are called forward.

♦

From Love Is Liberation: Five Contemplations for Daily Ethical Living (2026), courtesy of Parallax Press, parallax.org.

Our individual responses to these questions are shaped by our life experience, our values, and sometimes by our energy, health and well-being, and so much more. Whether we are aware of them or not, each of us probably already lives by a set of precepts, or principles and values. Many of us are guided by common precepts such as truthfulness, honesty, and refraining from stealing and cheating. From a tender age, we are taught these ways of becoming “good citizens” in the world, in the workplace, in our family, and with ourselves.

Some people take these precepts through formal vows, such as codes of school or religious conduct. For many, though, these vows can become wooden, flat, perfunctory, and then forgotten over time. We “set and forget” them and then feel bereft from inner guidance when we most need it. So how do we bring these precepts, this internal guidance system, into our daily life and call on them when we need them the most?

Over the years, in attending retreats with Thầy and the Plum Village community, I have come to understand that the precepts are not linear. Instead, each precept connects and is interdependent with all of the precepts. For example, the first precept on reverence for life is interdependent with the fifth precept on consuming mindfully. Since they are all interwoven, practicing one precept will impact your practice of the others. Not only are the precepts interconnected, but we are also interconnected to each other and all the elements in the cosmos. Because of all this, and because our actions have an impact on others whether we are aware of it or not, when you practice the precepts, you are not doing so for yourself alone, as a separate entity—you are doing so for all beings. What you consume and how you consume will have an impact on yourself, on others, and on the earth.

According to Thầy’s teachings on emptiness, your body isn’t just yours; your body belongs to your parents, society, and future generations. All of these have come together to manifest your body, including the trees, the clouds, and the oceans. Your body and your practice are manifestations of the whole cosmos. To practice the precepts is to support not only yourself but also your ancestors, your parents, future generations, and society. To practice the precepts is to recognize this interdependent relationship between you and the cosmos. The precepts are about cultivating conscious awareness and connectedness, especially now, in a society that has gone numb with divisiveness, too-muchness, and too-fastness.

The precepts are an invitation to be in touch with what is wholesome and beneficial in and around us. They are bells of mindfulness. Ultimately, the precepts are opportunities to live and grow a compassionate life of love, peace, and understanding. We might be challenged in our practice at times, and at those times we need to recommit ourselves and reconnect with spiritual friends who support us on the path toward living a healthy and wholesome life.

–Valerie Brown

Contemplations on the Five Mindfulness Trainings

Preamble to the Contemplations on the Five Mindfulness Trainings

Let us open to another way of understanding the Five Mindfulness Trainings, guiding principles for mindful and ethical living, which call us toward individual and collective awakening, compassion, and peace. We are interconnected. What happens in one part of the universe affects people everywhere. What happens to the Black body affects all bodies. We are called forward. Global pandemics, the climate crisis, social and economic oppression and upheaval are gateways to suffering worldwide, disproportionately impacting Black, Indigenous, and other people of color; disabled people; people currently and historically subject to poverty, war, and genocide; LGBTQIA+ people; people facing health inequities and premature death; people facing generational displacement; and people with historically socially marginalized identities, including those facing oppression because of their abilities, gender, or immigration status. They, we, are not alone. Our lives and livelihoods are interconnected. We are called forward.

We cannot exist independent of, for example, low-wage workers, health care workers, unhoused people, single mothers, undocumented people, the unemployed and underemployed, and similarly situated people. If one such person lives on the knife edge of racial, ethnic, social, structural, and systemic oppression and discrimination, we are all affected. We are called forward.

The practitioner dwells in the now, recognizing the dualistic nature of equanimity and instability, discrimination and nondiscrimination, ill-being and well-being. We practice right view and compassionate action, moving toward right insight. Aware of the interconnectedness and interdependence of all life, we courageously turn to practice wholeheartedly. We are called forward.

Lighting a stick of incense, listening to the sutras, sitting upright and solid, palms joined, the practitioner looks within, and in concentration the path and fruit of skillful action are revealed. We are called forward.

Speak aloud these words with the sangha voice, a true river of understanding.

Contemplation on the First Mindfulness Training: Acknowledging Beauty as Reverence for Life

Aware of the suffering caused by oppression and generational harm based on racial, cultural, social, and ethnic inferiority and superiority, I acknowledge the beauty and violence inherent in life. I vow to resist being complicit in systems and structures that continue to perpetuate injustice, violence, hatred, and delusion instead of reverence of life for marginalized groups and others. I recognize that each person contributes to my individual and our collective awakening, and to the co-creation of a world that celebrates and affirms differences and similarities. All living beings can teach me something, when I remember to pause, breathe, listen deeply with a calm and open mind and heart, and ask myself, “Is there more?” or “What else is here with me?” I honor and respect all life, guided by right view and right effort.

Contemplation on the Second Mindfulness Training: Belonging and Connecting as True Happiness

Aware of the suffering caused by ignorance and aversion of my own and others’ racial, ethnic, cultural, and social history, its legacy and how this affects me, I am committed to learning and connecting to these histories. Aware that there is no genetic or biological difference among racial and ethnic groups, and that these identities were socially constructed by one group to establish dominance over others, I will turn toward all forms of othering with the aspiration of transforming heart and mind. I know that this history has led to fragmentation inside and outside the body and mind and has brought much suffering to all beings. I will notice when emotions of belonging and othering arise, and I will ask myself, “Why?” Whatever feelings, perceptions, or mental formations arise in me, I will embrace and engage them with love in action. I am committed to practicing right resolve, right speech, right action, and right livelihood so I can help relieve this legacy of racial and social suffering. I will practice looking deeply to see that true happiness is not possible without true connection leading to belonging and understanding.

Contemplation on the Third Mindfulness Training: Cherishment as True Love

Aware of the suffering caused by discrimination and oppression, I vow to transform these seeds in myself, my sangha, and society. I recognize the ways in which I have benefitted or not benefitted, explicitly or implicitly, from systems and structures of injustice. I am aware of the legacy of violence, including unlawful police violence, perpetrated against people of various gender identities, expressions, and sexual orientations, Black people, indigenous people, people of color, disabled people, undocumented people, people suffering mental health challenges, and others who are marginalized. I am committed to looking tenderly at my suffering, knowing that I am not separate from others and that the seeds of suffering contain the seeds of joy. I am aware that narrow interpretations of intimate relationships constrain how we cherish each other in our expression of love, leaving many isolated and alienated. I am not afraid of bold love that fosters compassion, justice, and peace, and tender love that seeks understanding. I cherish this breath, body, mind, and moment as an act of healing for myself and for others. I cherish the liberation of all beings guided by the wisdom and the solidity of the sangha as my path of true love.

Contemplation on the Fourth Mindfulness Training: Vulnerability as Deep Listening and Loving Speech

Aware that vulnerability is the essence of our true nature, our humanness, I vow to risk listening for understanding rather than disagreement. I am committed to generous and courageous listening that bridges differences and supports others who may be different from me. When I am not able to understand others, I vow to come back to my breath and my body, and to offer myself gentle patience. I am aware that loving communication rests on honesty, compassion, and openness that align with my highest aspiration to alleviate suffering. When I have hurt others through my unskillful listening or speech, I vow to practice true beneficial regret, making a good apology that acknowledges what I have done and the harm caused, accepting responsibility and being accountable for my behavior, and offering sincere regret for my actions, knowing that this supports the other person and me. Through my practices of vulnerability, forgiveness, and deep listening, I know that my speech will be guided by love and understanding. Practicing in this way supports right speech and right action and guides me to right insight.

Contemplation on the Fifth Mindfulness Training: Welcoming as True Nourishing and Healing

Aware of the suffering caused by the consumption of an inadequate history of racial and ethnic forms of social segregation and injustice, I am committed to healing myself and the world. I am aware that my thoughts, perceptions, feelings, words, and actions may have been influenced by this history. I vow to understand how I have been influenced by embracing and denying this racial, social, and ethnic history of inferiority, superiority, and equality. I will cultivate joy to nourish me in this aspiration. I will practice mindfulness of the four kinds of nutriments to become aware of how edible foods, sense impressions, volition, and consciousness are all influenced by this history. Practicing with right energy and right resolve, my conscious consumption will be guided by right action that welcomes differences without discrimination. This right insight offers true welcoming on this path to nourish and heal myself, my ancestors, my descendants, my sangha, and society.

The Five Mindfulness Trainings keep us centered in life’s storms and joys and remind us that life is a precious gift. The Trainings are a path to liberation and transformation. Practicing these Trainings supports us toward racial and ethnic reconciliation and social change and heals deep suffering. The Five Mindfulness Trainings help us cross this shore of suffering and bring us to the side of true awakening and love. The Contemplations on the Five Mindfulness Trainings are a commentary to these foundational teachings and are meant to offer another way of understanding Thich Nhất Hạnh’s teachings to live an ethical life. We are called forward.

♦

From Love Is Liberation: Five Contemplations for Daily Ethical Living (2026), courtesy of Parallax Press, parallax.org.
